philosophers.name: John Stuart Mill
philosophers.coreQuestion: What produces the greatest well-being for the greatest number?
philosophers.keyArgument: Actions are right insofar as they promote happiness and wrong insofar as they produce the reverse. Mill refines Bentham by distinguishing quality of happiness — some pleasures are higher than others.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: Trolley Problem — pull the lever to save five at the cost of one?
philosophers.hook: Mill's father began his education at age 3. He read Greek by 8 and Latin by 9. He later had a complete nervous breakdown and credited poetry with saving his sanity.

philosophers.name: Immanuel Kant
philosophers.coreQuestion: What is my duty, and does this action respect the dignity of every person involved?
philosophers.keyArgument: Some actions are wrong regardless of consequences. The categorical imperative: act only according to rules you'd be willing to make universal. People must never be used merely as means to an end.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: Trolley Problem footbridge variant — push one person off a bridge to stop the trolley?
philosophers.hook: Kant was so punctual in his daily walk that neighbors set their clocks by him. He never traveled more than 40 miles from his birthplace his entire life.

philosophers.name: John Locke
philosophers.coreQuestion: What rights do people have that no government can legitimately take away?
philosophers.keyArgument: People have natural rights to life, liberty, and property that exist before government. Governments derive legitimacy only from the consent of the governed. When government violates natural rights, revolution is justified.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: If you mix your labor with something — land, an idea, a resource — do you own it? What happens when the system that defines ownership was itself built unjustly?
philosophers.hook: Locke's ideas were so dangerous that he published his Two Treatises anonymously. The American founders borrowed from him so heavily that some passages of the Declaration are nearly direct paraphrases.

philosophers.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
philosophers.coreQuestion: What does the community as a whole owe its members, and what do members owe the community?
philosophers.keyArgument: Legitimate authority comes from the general will — the collective interest of the community, not just the sum of individual interests. Rousseau disagreed with Locke: private property is a source of inequality, not freedom.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: If the majority votes for something that harms a minority, is it just? What's the difference between the will of all and the general will?
philosophers.hook: Rousseau abandoned all five of his children to orphanages, then wrote one of the most influential books on education ever published. He was aware of the contradiction.

philosophers.name: John Rawls
philosophers.coreQuestion: What rules would you choose if you didn't know your position in the society those rules would govern?
philosophers.keyArgument: The veil of ignorance: just rules are ones you'd agree to before knowing whether you'd be rich or poor, majority or minority, powerful or powerless. Inequalities are only justified if they benefit the least advantaged members of society.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: Veil of Ignorance — design a society knowing you might be born into any position within it.
philosophers.hook: Rawls served in WWII and witnessed the aftermath of Hiroshima. He later wrote that the atomic bombing could not be justified — a direct application of his own framework.

philosophers.name: Frederick Douglass
philosophers.coreQuestion: When a society's practice contradicts its stated principles, which one reveals its true character?
philosophers.keyArgument: The founding documents contain the philosophical standard by which American practice stands condemned. Douglass used Locke's own framework — natural rights, consent of the governed — to indict a system Locke's ideas were used to justify.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: What to the Slave is the Fourth of July? — If a document guarantees rights to all people, what does it mean that those rights are denied to millions?
philosophers.hook: Douglass taught himself to read using a spelling book and by tricking white children into writing lessons. He later became the most photographed American of the 19th century — he believed images of dignified Black men were a form of political argument.

philosophers.name: Peter Singer
philosophers.coreQuestion: If you can prevent something bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, are you obligated to do it?
philosophers.keyArgument: Geographic and emotional distance don't change moral obligation. But individual obligation must be understood alongside the demandingness problem, systemic causes of suffering, and collective action failures — Singer himself argues for systemic change, not just individual guilt.
philosophers.thoughtExperiment: The Drowning Child — you pass a shallow pond where a child is drowning. You could save them but ruin your clothes. Singer then asks: what's the moral difference between that child and one dying of preventable disease across the world?
philosophers.hook: Singer is one of the most controversial philosophers alive. He donates a significant portion of his own income to effective charities — and argues his framework still doesn't demand enough of him.

units.title: Reconstruction
units.closingPrompt: What is owed to people whose labor built a society that excluded them from its benefits?

philosophyFriday.hypothetical: A person is forced to build a house for someone else for twenty years without pay. They are then freed but left with nothing. The person who owns the house says 'I'm not forcing you to work anymore — isn't that enough?' Is it?
historicalPrompts: If a government allows a serious wrong to happen for a long time and then stops it, does it owe anything to the people who were wronged? Does your answer change if the people harmed had no power to hold the government accountable?
If someone benefits for years from a serious wrong done to another person — even if they didn't commit the wrong themselves — do they owe anything to the person who was harmed?

Imagine a society that has been run unjustly for a long time finally decides to change. Is it enough to simply stop doing the unjust things, or does a just society have to actively fix what the injustice caused?
philosophyFriday.frameworkFocus: Utilitarianism vs. Deontology — does the obligation to repair come from consequences or from duty?

units.title: Gilded Age
units.closingPrompt: What does a person owe to the workers whose labor built their wealth?

philosophyFriday.hypothetical: A person discovers an uninhabited island and spends years clearing it, building on it, and making it productive. Others arrive later and do the same work for wages the first person sets. Who owns the island? Who decides?
historicalPrompts: Do people who accumulate enormous wealth through systems they didn't design alone owe anything to the people whose labor built that wealth?
Is there a point at which private property becomes incompatible with the general good? Who gets to decide where that point is?
philosophyFriday.frameworkFocus: Locke's labor theory of property meets utilitarian questions about wealth distribution

units.title: Progressive Era & New Deal
units.closingPrompt: When individual action fails, what can the government justly demand of its citizens?

philosophyFriday.hypothetical: A neighborhood has a serious pollution problem. Each household contributes a small amount. No single household is responsible. No single household can fix it alone. What, if anything, can the community require individuals to do?
historicalPrompts: When markets fail and people suffer, does the government have a moral obligation to intervene — or does intervention violate individual rights?
Is it just to tax some people heavily to provide for others who cannot provide for themselves?
philosophyFriday.frameworkFocus: Rousseau's general will and Rawls' difference principle — what do just institutions owe the least advantaged?

units.title: World War II & Holocaust
units.closingPrompt: What do ordinary people owe to strangers in danger, even at cost to themselves?

philosophyFriday.openingType: Historical — deployed later in unit after content established
historicalPrompts: If you know a serious wrong is being committed and you do nothing, are you morally responsible for what happens?
Can a soldier or government official be morally excused for following orders they knew were wrong? Does it matter whether refusing would have changed the outcome?
Was dropping the atomic bomb on civilian populations justified? Which framework gives the most defensible answer — and where does that framework break down?
philosophyFriday.frameworkFocus: Kant's categorical imperative applied to atrocity — some acts cannot be justified by consequences. Mill's calculus tested at its limits.
philosophyFriday.note: Deploy philosophical prompt after students have sufficient historical context. This unit requires content before philosophy, not philosophy before content.

units.title: Civil Rights
units.closingPrompt: When a society's laws are unjust, what do citizens owe the law — and what does the law owe them?

philosophyFriday.openingType: Straight Historical Prompt — full Option 3 deployment
historicalPrompts: If a government's laws contradict its founding principles, which one reveals its true character?
Is civil disobedience ever morally required — not just permitted, but required?
What is the difference between a law that is legal and a law that is just? Who gets to decide?
philosophyFriday.frameworkFocus: Douglass applies Lockean natural rights to indict the system. Rawls' veil of ignorance tests whether Jim Crow could survive rational scrutiny. Kant on the duty to resist unjust law.

units.title: Modern Times
units.closingPrompt: What do we owe people we will never meet, in places we will never go, in times that haven't happened yet?

historicalPrompts: Do wealthy nations have a moral obligation to address poverty in poor ones — or does national sovereignty limit moral obligation at borders?
Do future generations have rights that current policy is obligated to protect?
Is affirmative action consistent with a genuine social contract — or does it violate it?
philosophyFriday.frameworkFocus: Singer's contemporary utilitarianism applied to global obligation. Rawls on distributive justice across generations. Students generate their own prompts as capstone.

phase1.title: The Toolkit
phase1.description: Introduce utilitarianism and deontology through pure hypotheticals before connecting to content. Students receive reference card.
keyMoves: Trolley problem — isolates the utilitarian/deontological split
Footbridge variant — most students switch intuitions, creating productive confusion
Anonymous writing, class rates quality of reasoning, frameworks arrive as explanation

phase2.title: Applied to History
phase2.description: Frameworks become analytical tools applied to historical questions. Disguised prompts reveal that abstract and historical reasoning are the same activity.
keyMoves: Disguised historical prompts — students argue a thought experiment, then discover it was the real question
Philosopher introduced when unit content most needs them
Before-and-after revision shows students their own thinking change

phase3.title: Live Questions
phase3.description: Students apply full toolkit to contemporary questions. Capstone: students generate their own prompts.
keyMoves: Students identify which framework a public argument is using
Students recognize when someone switches frameworks for convenience
Students distinguish empirical from normative claims in live debates
Capstone: student-generated prompts argued with two named frameworks

writingProtocol.title: Anonymous Writing & Quality Recognition
writingProtocol.inspiration: Pirsig, Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
principles: Recognition of quality precedes instruction in technique
Anonymity removes status — work stands alone
Desire to understand technique comes from desire to replicate recognized quality
Writing is a conduit to thinking, not the end product
sequence: Prompt issued Thursday or end of previous Friday
Friday: 4–5 pieces read aloud, no names
Class rates each: Strong / Medium / Weak — reasoning quality only, not grammar
Discussion surfaces patterns in strong pieces
Framework introduced as explanation of what they already noticed
Exit: rewrite one sentence from a weak argument using the framework
promptDesignPrinciples: No obviously correct answer, but not infinitely open
Forces a choice — defend or challenge, not discuss
Short — one or two sentences maximum
Answerable from intuition, deepened by knowledge
writingProtocol.aiNote: AI produces surface quality without the experience of reasoning. Students who use AI skip the part that does something for them. The anonymous reading often reveals this — assembled writing feels different from argued writing. This is teachable, not just a disciplinary issue.
